To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the Universal Medical Language System (UMLS) and the Gene Ontologies (GO) are not ontologies in the sense in which this term has been defined in the context of the theory of granulation; 2) these resources can be improved by applying this theory and the associated principles; 3) this improvement is likely to be accompanied by an increase in the efficiency and robustness associated with software applications which use these resources.

the Gene Ontology and the Unified Medical Language System do not meet the criteria for well-constructed terminologies, and that the theory of granules provides a useful tool for the analysis of ontologies.
(i) The UMLS is not an ontology; (ii) The UMLS does not meet the criteria for being an ontology; and (iii) The Gene Ontology does not meet the minimal criteria for being an adequate ontology.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a theory of ontologies, and the development of an ontology engineering methodology, which is founded upon this theory.
the question of what is the best way to represent the knowledge of a domain in an ontological system.
the development of an approach that can be applied to the design and construction of ontologies that will be more useful in practice.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

we are not yet in a position to say that the UMLS and the Gene Ontologies are well-constructed, and that the theory of granulated partitions is a valuable tool to help us to improve the situation in the future.

the UMLS and the Gene Ontologies, despite their widespread adoption and utility, do not conform to the basic principles of ontology design, and that this is a major cause of their limitations in terms of their ability to support accurate and robust reasoning.
the UMLS and the GO are not ontologies in any sense that is of interest for the development of software applications.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have provided evidence that the current ontologies in the biomedical domain are inadequate and that the principles for constructing ontologies are not being properly applied.
, in the biomedical domain at least, the ontologies we have are not yet ontologies at all.
we are in urgent need of a new generation of biomedical terminologies and ontologies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ontologies should be built in a way that they can support the creation of software applications that can handle real world problems.
, in the context of the biomedical domain, ontologies must be constructed with a view to the real world of the domain.
, in order for ontologies to be effective and efficient tools for representing and reasoning with knowledge, they must be built in such a way that they are consistent with the structure of reality.
